title: Bluffs and semi-bluffs
summary: Which hands to bluff with, how often, and why a semi-bluff beats a pure bluff.

idea.text:
A **bluff** is a bet with a weak hand that wins only if the opponent folds. A **semi-bluff** is a bet with a draw: if the opponent calls, you still have outs to make the best hand.

A semi-bluff wins two ways (a fold or hitting), so on the flop and turn it is almost always better than a pure bluff.

how-often.text:
How many folds a bluff needs to pay: **bet / (pot + bet)**.
- A half-pot bet: the opponent must fold **33%** of the time.
- A pot-size bet: **50%**.

On the river, a balanced betting range keeps bluffs at **bet / (pot + 2 × bet)** of it: with a pot-size bet that is a third, one bluff for every two value hands.

labels: River bluff with a blocker: the ace makes AK and AQ less likely for the opponent

pick.text:
Good bluffing hands: draws (semi-bluffs), hands with **blockers** to the opponent's strong hands, hands with no showdown value. Bad ones: middle pairs that already beat some of the opponent's bluffs; check those.

Bluff one opponent who is able to fold, on boards where your range looks stronger. Against calling stations and several opponents, bluffs hardly work.

q-folds.q: You bet the pot on the river as a bluff. How often must the opponent fold for it to pay?

t1.q: Why is a semi-bluff better than a pure bluff?
options: It wins both by a fold and by hitting
t1.explain: A semi-bluff is a bet with a draw: if called, you can still make your hand.

t2.q: How many folds does a half-pot bluff need?

t3.explain: A calling station hardly ever folds, so bluffing them loses money.
